card_description: A Neolithic chambered tomb from the 3rd millennium BC with a trapezoidal stone cairn. It is classified as a Severn-Cotswold type, a style found across western Britain.
description: Parc Cwm long cairn, also known as Parc le Breos burial chamber, is a partly restored Neolithic chambered tomb on the Gower Peninsula, Wales. Identified in 1937 as a Severn-Cotswold type of chambered long barrow, it was built around 5,850 years before present during the early Neolithic. The monument features a trapezoidal cairn of rubble with a cromlech (megalithic burial chamber). Located approximately 12 km west-south-west of Swansea in Coed y Parc Cwm at Parc le Breos, it represents an important example of Neolithic burial architecture in South Wales.[1]

description: The Ringlemere barrow is an archaeological site near Sandwich in the English county of Kent most famous as being the find site of the Ringlemere gold cup [1]. No contemporary burials have been found at the site although later Iron Age ones have since been found along with a Saxon cemetery [1]. Excavation work has continued at the site, funded by English Heritage, the BBC, the British Museum and the Kent Archaeological Society [1]. This work has indicated that the now ploughed-away barrow was as high as 5m and had a diameter of more than 40m [1]. The flat-bottomed ditch that surrounded it was 5–6 m wide and 1.35 m deep [1]. Considerable evidence of much earlier Neolithic activity has now been found on the site including by far the largest assemblage of grooved ware in the county [1].

card_description: The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros was reportedly first identified in 1856 by Carlos Ribeiro but he did not have a chance to carry out excavations until 1876 after receiving approval from the landowner.
description: The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros, also known as the Anta do Senhor da Serra, is a megalithic dolmen situated near Belas and Queluz in the Lisbon District of Portugal [1]. It is believed to date back to the late-Neolithic and early-Chalcolithic eras (4000-2500 BC) [1]. The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros, the Anta da Estria, and the Anta do Monte Abraão are a short distance from each other and are collectively known as the Antas de Belas [1]. The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros was reportedly first identified in 1856 by Carlos Ribeiro but he did not have a chance to carry out excavations until 1876 after receiving approval from the landowner [1]. The burial chamber was at that time already in bad condition, having only three upright support stones, with one apparently having two anthropomorphic figures engraved on it [1]. Items found by Ribeiro during his excavations are kept in the Geological Museum in Lisbon [1]. They include a stone axe, flint tools, utensils for domestic use, vases, and human and animal bones [1].

It was excavated by Augustus Pitt Rivers between 1888 and 1891 and is a Scheduled Monument.

description: Devil's Lapful is a Neolithic long cairn in Kielder Forest, Northumberland, dating to approximately 3400-2400 BC. One of few surviving long cairns in Northumberland, it measures 60 by 14 metres and stands 2 metres high, constructed of rounded boulders with stone slabs and smaller stones at the edges. Oriented north-northeast to south-southwest on a hillside slope, the cairn likely served as a communal burial site for a local community over several generations. First examined in the 1930s by Newbigin with inconclusive results, the site shows evidence of later quarrying for a nearby sheep fold. It has been designated a scheduled monument.

description: Devetashka Cave is a massive karst formation near the village of Devetaki in northern Bulgaria, measuring approximately 2 km in length with a cavernous entrance hall reaching 60 m in height and seven natural ceiling openings known as 'the eyes'. Archaeological evidence reveals nearly continuous human occupation spanning 70,000 years, from the Middle Paleolithic to the Late Neolithic. The sediment layers have yielded one of the richest sources of Neolithic cultural artifacts (6th-4th millennium BC) in Bulgaria, alongside Paleolithic flint tools, Bronze Age battle axes, and Iron Age weapons. Declared a natural landmark in 1996, the cave also shelters nearly 30,000 bats, though military use in the 1950s for petroleum storage damaged some formations.

The seaside sites of Huaynuná and Las Haldas are found about 20 kilometres north and south of the mouth of the Casma River on the coast [1]. The area of the Casma/Sechin culture extended about 40 kilometres inland from the sea [1]. By 3000 BC, at a few locations in coastal Peru, including the Casma/Sechin valleys, a sizable population was present and undertaking large projects such as building pyramids and other ceremonial and monumental structures [1]. Radiocarbon dating indicates a plaza at Sechin Bajo was constructed in 3500 BCE [1].

It is a Doric peripteral temple, and is located at the north-west side of the Agora of Athens, on top of the Agoraios Kolonos hill [1]. description_citations.claim: Iximche was the capital of the Late Postclassic Kaqchikel Maya kingdom from 1470 until its abandonment in 1524. The architecture included pyramid-temples, palaces and two Mesoamerican ballcourts. Excavators uncovered poorly preserved painted murals and evidence of human sacrifice. The ruins were declared a Guatemalan National Monument in the 1960s and the site has a museum displaying sculptures and ceramics.
